objective: By the end of this lesson you can explain what makes an approach nonprecision, choose and brief the right chart and line of minima, adjust the MDA and visibility for category and conditions, teach a planned descent from the FAF to the MDA, VDP and MAP, fly and talk through VOR, LOC and RNAV (GPS) LNAV or LP approaches full panel and partial panel, and spot and fix a learner's chart, radio, checklist, flying and MDA errors.
why: A nonprecision approach gives course guidance but no glidepath, so the pilot builds the descent and guards the MDA alone, and below the MDA there is no implicit obstacle protection [[33:400|AIM 5-4-5a7]] [[33:413|AIM 5-4-5i]]. A descent rate over about 1,000 fpm below 1,000 ft AGL is unacceptable, and a constant-rate descent is safer than a string of level-offs [[29:177|IPH 4-37]] [[29:165|IPH 4-25]]. The PTS also has you fly one of these approaches without the gyro attitude and heading indicators, because of fatal spatial disorientation accidents after those instruments failed in cloud [[FAA-S-8081-9E:16|PTS Introduction]] [[FAA-S-8081-9E:40|PTS Area VIII NOTE]].

warmup: Think first: your instrument learner flies the VOR approach perfectly to the FAF, then dives at 1,200 fpm to the MDA, levels off 4 miles out, and at the first glimpse of lights pushes the nose down. Which of those habits is legal, which is unsafe, and what would you teach before the next flight?

key_terms.def: An approach with course deviation guidance but no glidepath deviation guidance, such as VOR, NDB and LNAV [[33:400|AIM 5-4-5a7]]; also LOC, TACAN and ASR [[29:190|IPH 4-50]].
Course and glidepath guidance that need not meet ICAO precision standards, such as LNAV/VNAV and LPV [[33:400|AIM 5-4-5a7]], published with a DA [[33:418|AIM 5-4-5m6(b)]].
The lowest altitude, in feet MSL, to which descent is authorized on final or while circling when no electronic glideslope is provided [[29:159|IPH 4-19]].

The altitude where the missed approach must start if the required visual reference is not established [[29:160|IPH 4-20]]; a momentary descent below it during the missed is protected [[33:418|AIM 5-4-5m5(a)]].
A point, marked V, on a straight-in nonprecision final from which a stabilized visual descent from the MDA to touchdown can start [[33:413|AIM 5-4-5h]] [[2:117|Chart Users' Guide p 117]].
An advisory angle from the FAF or stepdown fix to the threshold crossing height; it does not guarantee obstacle protection below the MDA [[33:413|AIM 5-4-5k]] [[33:414|AIM 5-4-5k2]].
A fix between the FAF and the airport that allows a lower minimum altitude after passing an obstacle [[23:40|IFH 1-21]].
On a nonprecision approach, a fix, a NAVAID, or a time after the FAF at which the missed approach begins [[29:190|IPH 4-50]].
A grouping by VREF, or 1.3 VSO at maximum certificated landing weight if no VREF is given: A, B, C, D or E [[60:724|14 CFR 97.3]].

The straight-in MDA or DA expressed as height above the touchdown zone elevation [[2:120|Chart Users' Guide p 120]]; TDZE is the highest point in the first 3,000 ft of the landing surface [[2:122|Chart Users' Guide p 122]].
Flying the final segment as one constant-rate descent instead of several level-offs at stepdown fixes; some countries require it on nonprecision approaches [[29:165|IPH 4-25]].
A WAAS lateral-only line of minima with localizer-like sensitivity near the runway, flown to an MDA, not a DA [[33:416|AIM 5-4-5m1(d)]].

chunks.title: Nonprecision, APV or precision, and choosing the approach

body.p: The Instrument lesson IR.VI.A covers the pilot's side of this Task; this lesson adds how you teach it. Start by fixing the words, because the sources sort approaches into three groups by the guidance given on final [[33:400|AIM 5-4-5a7]] [[29:190|IPH 4-50]].

head: Group
Guidance on final
Minimum
Examples
rows: Precision approach (PA)
Course and glidepath deviation that meet ICAO Annex 10 precision standards [[33:400|AIM 5-4-5a7]]
PAR, ILS, GLS [[33:400|AIM 5-4-5a7]]
Approach with vertical guidance (APV)
Course and glidepath deviation, not required to meet the precision standards [[33:400|AIM 5-4-5a7]]
LNAV/VNAV, LPV, baro-VNAV, LDA with glidepath [[33:400|AIM 5-4-5a7]]
Nonprecision approach (NPA)
Course deviation only, no glidepath deviation [[33:400|AIM 5-4-5a7]]

body.p: **Where the labels differ.** For alternate planning the IPH counts APVs as non-precision, because they do not meet ICAO Annex 10 precision standards [[29:146|IPH 4-6]], and it says LPV is not a precision approach even with minima as low as 200 ft HAT [[29:203|IPH 4-63]]. The PTS splits the Tasks by the minimum: a nonprecision approach goes to a published MDA without approved vertical guidance, a precision approach to a DA with approved vertical guidance [[FAA-S-8081-9E:11|PTS Introduction]]. So for the checkride, VOR, LOC, LNAV and LP belong to this Task; LPV and LNAV/VNAV flown to a DA belong to Task B.

**An advisory glidepath does not change the group.** A published VDA does not make an approach an APV, since it is still flown to an MDA and was not evaluated with a glidepath [[33:400|AIM 5-4-5a7]]. The PTS lets the applicant use systems that show advisory vertical guidance on nonprecision approaches without restriction [[FAA-S-8081-9E:11|PTS Introduction]].

**Selection of the appropriate instrument approach procedure chart.** At a civil airport the pilot uses a standard procedure prescribed in 14 CFR part 97 for that airport [[60:471|14 CFR 91.175(a)]], and civil charts show (FAA) at the top [[33:397|AIM 5-4-5a]]. Weather, wind and field conditions decide which approaches can be used; at airports with only one or a few approaches the wrong mix of wind and visibility can rule them all out [[29:142|IPH 4-2]]. The approach to expect comes from ATIS or the controller, but it is not a clearance, and the pilot tells ATC at once if unable to fly it [[33:397|AIM 5-4-4a]] [[33:397|AIM 5-4-4b]].

bullets: The title names the equipment for final: a slash means both systems, "or" means either, and a letter in place of a runway means circling only [[33:398|AIM 5-4-5a3(a)]].
Also read the notes, plan view and PBN or equipment boxes, because the slash and /DME are being removed from titles [[33:398|AIM 5-4-5a3(a)]] [[33:399|AIM 5-4-5a3(g)]].
"Or GPS" overlays may be flown with GPS, but LOC, LDA and SDF procedures may not [[33:95|AIM 1-1-17b5(a)]].
Two approaches of the same type to one runway get letters from Z backward, and Z normally has the lower minimums [[29:149|IPH 4-9]] [[29:151|IPH 4-11]].
"Cleared approach" with no type named lets the pilot fly any authorized approach at that airport [[33:420|AIM 5-4-6e]].

callout.text: Application: hand the learner all the charts for the destination, the ATIS and the airplane's equipment list, and ask which approach and which line they will fly, and why. Choosing is an element of its own (K1a), and a wrong choice spoils every step after it.

check.q: Your learner's airplane, with a non-WAAS GPS and no baro-VNAV, is cleared for an RNAV (GPS) approach with LPV, LNAV/VNAV and LNAV lines. Which line can they use, and does it belong to this Task?
check.a: LNAV, flown to an MDA, since LPV needs WAAS and LNAV/VNAV needs approach-approved baro-VNAV or WAAS [[33:416|AIM 5-4-5m1(b)]] [[33:416|AIM 5-4-5m1(c)]] [[33:416|AIM 5-4-5m1(e)]]. An MDA line without approved vertical guidance is a nonprecision approach [[FAA-S-8081-9E:11|PTS Introduction]].

chunks.title: Reading the chart top to bottom: Monroeville RNAV (GPS) RWY 3

body.p: **Pertinent information on the selected instrument approach chart.** FAA charts use the Pilot Briefing Information format, presented in a logical order that makes briefing easy [[29:149|IPH 4-9]]. The communication strip lists frequencies in the order of use [[29:151|IPH 4-11]]. A single pilot should still brief the approach to verify the setup [[29:175|IPH 4-35]], and the briefing doubles as a checklist [[29:182|IPH 4-42]]. Application: teach every learner to brief every chart the same way, aloud.

What to find
On the Monroeville chart

Airport sketch

body.p: The IFH caption calls this a VOR or GPS approach, but the chart itself is titled RNAV (GPS) RWY 3 and is dated 2010 to 2011 [[23:305|IFH Figure 10-8]]. Teach from what the chart says, and fly only current charts.

**Failure to have essential knowledge of the information on the instrument approach chart.** It looks like an early descent, a course reversal flown on a NoPT leg, the wrong line of minima, or a learner who does not know the missed approach when the MAP arrives. The usual cause is a briefing that skipped items or never happened. The fix is a full briefing before the IAF, including the missed approach, because the missed comes when workload is highest [[23:312|IFH 10-21]] [[29:182|IPH 4-42]].

callout.text: Brief in chart order: title and NAVAID, course, TDZE, notes, missed approach, frequencies, plan view and MSA, profile altitudes and fixes, minimums for your category, airport sketch [[2:98|Chart Users' Guide p 98]] [[29:149|IPH 4-9]].

check.q: Your learner briefs the Monroeville minimums as 840-1 but skipped the notes. The CTAF gives no altimeter setting. What was missed?
check.a: The note to use Middleton Field's setting when the local one is not received, and its own line of minima, 900-1 for Categories A and B [[23:305|IFH Figure 10-8]]. With no authorized setting at all, the approach would not be authorized [[33:399|AIM 5-4-5a4]].

chunks.title: MDA or DA: the RNAV (GPS) lines and stepdown fixes

body.p: An RNAV (GPS) chart can carry LPV, LNAV/VNAV, LP, LNAV and circling lines, and the approach clearance lets the pilot use any line the aircraft is certified for [[33:415|AIM 5-4-5m]]. The minima box shows what kind of altitude each line is: DA for lines with vertical guidance, MDA for lateral-only LNAV and LP [[33:418|AIM 5-4-5m6(b)]].

body.p: **The same number can mean two things.** On the Oklahoma City chart, LNAV/VNAV and LNAV both read 1580/50 with a HAT of 303 [[29:164|IPH Figure 4-12]]. As a DA, 1580 is where the missed approach starts on the glidepath, and obstacle clearance allows a momentary descent below it during the transition to the missed [[33:418|AIM 5-4-5m5(a)]]. As an MDA, 1580 is a floor: no descent below it unless 14 CFR 91.175 is met [[33:418|AIM 5-4-5m6(b)]].

**Stepdowns.** Stepdown altitudes inside the final segment apply when flying an MDA line, not an LPV or LNAV/VNAV DA line; outside the final segment they apply to every approach [[33:401|AIM 5-4-5b5]]. If a stepdown fix cannot be identified, its altitude becomes the MDA, unless higher circling minimums apply and a circle is required [[23:40|IFH 1-21]].

**LP is not a backup LPV.** LP is published only where terrain or obstacles prevent vertical guidance, and only when it beats LNAV; any WAAS glidepath shown on LP is advisory and the barometric altimeter stays primary [[33:416|AIM 5-4-5m1(d)]]. Receivers do not fail down once the approach is active: with only a vertical flag the pilot may elect LNAV minima if the operating rules allow, and exceeding the lateral limit on LP means a missed approach [[33:105|AIM 1-1-18d2]].

callout.text: In rare cases the LNAV line has a lower HAT than a line with a glidepath. That is a clear sign that obstacles below the MDA must be seen; the glidepath may then be used only as a VDA to the LNAV MDA, with every nonprecision rule applied at the MDA [[29:163|IPH 4-23]].

check.q: Flying the LNAV line at Oklahoma City with WAAS advisory guidance, your learner says, "It is 1580 either way, so I can dip a little as I go missed." What do you teach?
check.a: Only a DA allows a momentary descent below it while starting the missed approach [[33:418|AIM 5-4-5m5(a)]]. LNAV is an MDA line, and with advisory guidance the pilot must stay at or above every published altitude using the barometric altimeter [[33:418|AIM 5-4-5m6(b)]] [[29:163|IPH 4-23]].

chunks.title: Select, tune, identify and check: VOR, LOC and GPS

body.p: **Selection, tuning, identification, and determination of operational status of ground and aircraft navigation equipment.** If the approach has a primary NAVAID, brief it, set it in the right radio and positively identify it before using it for course guidance [[29:157|IPH 4-17]]. Set up for a vacuum or electrical failure too: if only Nav 1 works on battery or emergency power, put the primary final approach NAVAID in Nav 1 [[29:175|IPH 4-35]].

head: System
Select and tune
Identify and confirm status
rows: VOR
All VOR approaches need working VOR equipment; DME in the title means operable DME to fly it from the FAF [[29:206|IPH 4-66]] [[29:209|IPH 4-69]]

Morse code, or a recorded voice ID followed by the word VOR, is the only positive ID [[33:68|AIM 1-1-3c]]; unless maintained under an approved procedure, a VOR check within the preceding 30 days for IFR [[60:470|14 CFR 91.171(a)(2)]]
Localizer
Aligned within 3° of the runway, at least 250 ft obstacle clearance on final [[29:216|IPH 4-76]]
Three-letter identifier preceded by I, such as I-DIA [[33:79|AIM 1-1-9b4]]
Back course
Use only where a back course procedure is published and ATC authorizes it [[33:79|AIM 1-1-9b3]]
Reverse sensing on a VOR-type indicator; ignore any glideslope; an HSI set to the front course removes reverse sensing [[29:216|IPH 4-76]]
GPS
Retrieve the whole procedure by name from a current database; no manually entered waypoints [[33:417|AIM 5-4-5m2]] [[33:96|AIM 1-1-17b5(e)(8)]]
RAIM prediction before flight [[33:97|AIM 1-1-17b5(g)(2)]]; armed by 30 NM [[33:96|AIM 1-1-17b5(e)(3)]]; approach active before the FAWP [[33:98|AIM 1-1-17b5(g)(6)]]
Any NAVAID
Check NOTAMs for the airport [[29:142|IPH 4-2]] and its NAVAIDs
No ID, or a TEST code, means maintenance and an unreliable signal; never fly a procedure NOTAMed out of service, even with an ID [[33:87|AIM 1-1-11]]

bullets: GPS not in approach mode by the FAWP, or a RAIM alert before it: do not descend; fly to the MAWP, go missed and tell ATC [[33:98|AIM 1-1-17b5(g)(7)]].
RAIM alert after the FAWP: climb and fly the missed approach [[33:98|AIM 1-1-17b5(g)(8)]].
WAAS: once the approach is active the receiver announces the best service, such as LP available or LNAV available; fly the matching line [[33:105|AIM 1-1-18d2]].

VOR pilot errors include careless tuning and identification, no receiver accuracy check, ignoring TO/FROM during course reversals, overcontrolling near the station and chasing the CDI [[23:257|IFH 9-14]] [[23:259|IFH 9-16]].

body.p: The Daytona Beach LOC BC RWY 25R shows why setup is a lesson of its own: back course with DME or radar required, "Disregard glideslope indications," and all MDAs raised 20 ft when the Ormond Beach altimeter setting is used [[29:229|IPH Figure 4-60]]. A learner who expects normal sensing on a VOR-type indicator will correct the wrong way, because the back course reverses it [[29:216|IPH 4-76]].

callout.text: Application: make the setup a spoken item: "109.7, I-DAB identified, in Nav 1, back course, expect reverse sensing, glideslope ignored." When the learner says it aloud you hear the misunderstanding before it shows on the needle [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].

check.q: Your learner sets up the Daytona LOC BC RWY 25R on a standard VOR-type indicator. What should they expect, and what should they ignore?
check.a: Reverse sensing, and any glideslope signal; the chart itself says to disregard glideslope indications [[29:216|IPH 4-76]] [[29:229|IPH Figure 4-60]].

chunks.title: Talking to ATC and following the clearance

body.p: **Radio communications with ATC and compliance with ATC clearances, instructions, and procedures.** Teach each clearance case by name, so the learner knows what to do before it happens.

head: Situation
What the learner does
rows: Cleared for the approach via a holding fix
Fly the last assigned route and the published feeder route to the IAF; a direct route must be stated as "direct"; if unsure, ask at once [[33:420|AIM 5-4-6a]] [[33:420|AIM 5-4-6c]]
Radar vectors and an approach clearance
Do not turn inbound before the approach clearance [[33:396|AIM 5-4-3b1(c)]]; keep the last assigned altitude until established on a published segment [[60:474|14 CFR 91.175(i)]]
Course reversal charted

Fly it unless cleared straight-in [[33:421|AIM 5-4-6h4]]; no procedure turn after a vector to final, on a timed approach from a holding fix or on a NoPT route unless ATC clears it [[60:474|14 CFR 91.175(j)]]
Cannot fly the approach ATC advised
Tell ATC immediately [[33:397|AIM 5-4-4b]]
Not in radar contact
Report leaving the FAF inbound [[33:377|AIM 5-3-3]]
Missed approach
Report it and request clearance for what comes next [[33:377|AIM 5-3-3]] [[33:451|AIM 5-4-21f]]
Airport without a tower
After "change to advisory frequency approved," announce the approach, the position and FAF inbound [[33:397|AIM 5-4-4d]]

body.p: The IPH lists the usual self-announce calls on the CTAF: 4 to 10 minutes before the IAF, departing the IAF, procedure turn inbound, FAF inbound with the runway and any circling direction, and short final [[29:156|IPH 4-16]]. ATC will not clear the next IFR arrival until the aircraft ahead has canceled IFR, and the pilot must start that cancellation [[29:155|IPH 4-15]] [[29:156|IPH 4-16]].

**Incorrect communications procedures or noncompliance with ATC clearances or instructions.** Typical forms: descending on a vector before being established, a procedure turn on a NoPT leg, accepting a clearance not understood, and no missed approach report. When uncertain of a clearance, the pilot must ask ATC immediately [[60:450|14 CFR 91.123(a)]]. A learner who feels rushed on vectors can ask for a delay or a vector that gives more time to configure [[30:47|RMH 6-4]].

callout.text: Application: play ATC from the right seat, including a vector across final with no warning. The AIM tells the pilot to query the controller when crossing is imminent and no one has said so [[33:396|AIM 5-4-3b1(b)]].

check.q: On a vector 10 NM outside the FAF your learner hears "cleared RNAV Runway 3 approach" and starts down to the FAF altitude at once. Right or wrong?
check.a: Wrong. On a vector, keep the last assigned altitude until established on a published segment of the approach [[60:474|14 CFR 91.175(i)]] [[33:421|AIM 5-4-6h1]].

body.p: **Appropriate aircraft configuration, airspeed, and checklist items.** Approach planning includes working out approach speeds and power settings [[29:142|IPH 4-2]]. A stabilized approach keeps speed, descent rate, vertical path and configuration constant in the final stages; it is strongly recommended for propeller airplanes, and low-altitude configuration changes should be limited to easy ones [[29:177|IPH 4-37]]. Crossing the FAF of a nonprecision approach at the proper airspeed, altitude and configuration is extremely important [[29:159|IPH 4-19]].

head: Point
Configuration and speed

Speed and power planned [[29:142|IPH 4-2]]
Weather, NOTAMs, radios and automation set; the briefing confirms the setup [[29:175|IPH 4-35]]
Before the FAF
Slow to the descent airspeed in level flight, configure and trim [[23:178|IFH 7-17]], so the FAF is crossed at the proper speed and configuration [[29:159|IPH 4-19]]
Approach checklist; MDA set in the altitude preselector, rounded up if it moves in 100 ft steps [[29:176|IPH 4-36]]

Reduce power and lower the nose to hold the speed; in a constant-rate descent the VSI is primary for pitch and airspeed for power [[23:178|IFH 7-17]]

Set the missed approach altitude once level [[29:176|IPH 4-36]]

body.p: Speed is a minimums item too: flying faster than the category's upper limit means using the higher category's minimums [[29:148|IPH 4-8]].

**Failure to accomplish checklist items.** Watch for a GPS left in terminal mode, a wrong altimeter setting, flaps or gear not set, or a missed approach altitude never set. If the GPS approach mode is not armed by 2 NM before the FAWP it will not go active; then the pilot must not descend, but flies to the MAWP and goes missed [[33:96|AIM 1-1-17b5(e)(7)]] [[33:98|AIM 1-1-17b5(g)(7)]]. The PTS accepts reviewing a checklist after the items are done when reading it during the maneuver would be unsafe or impracticable for a single pilot [[FAA-S-8081-9E:16|PTS Introduction]].

callout.text: Application: teach a flow first and the printed checklist to confirm it, with each item said aloud. In the learner-tells-learner-does step the thinking is done out loud, so you hear the item that was skipped [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].

check.q: Your learner reaches the FAF still at cruise speed and starts slowing, lowering flaps and descending all at once. What do you teach?
check.a: Slow and configure before the FAF so it is crossed at the proper speed and configuration [[29:159|IPH 4-19]]; large speed and configuration changes late in the approach degrade situational awareness [[29:177|IPH 4-37]].

body.p: **Adjustments applied to the published MDA and visibility criteria for the aircraft approach category.** Category comes from VREF, or 1.3 VSO at maximum certificated landing weight if no VREF is given: A below 91 knots, B 91 to below 121, C 121 to below 141, D 141 to below 166 [[60:724|14 CFR 97.3]].

bullets: An airplane is certified in one category and may never use a slower category's minimums [[29:148|IPH 4-8]].

Faster than the category limit means the higher category: a Category A airplane flying a straight-in at 130 knots uses Category C. Overweight returns, inoperative flaps and icing are examples that can force this [[29:148|IPH 4-8]].
The authorized MDA is the highest of the procedure's MDA, the one prescribed for the pilot in command, and the one for the equipment available and used [[60:471|14 CFR 91.175(b)]].

Remote altimeter settings: at Monroeville the Middleton setting raises the LNAV MDA from 840 to 900 for every category and the Category D visibility from 1¼ to 1½ [[23:305|IFH Figure 10-8]]; at Daytona Beach the Ormond Beach setting adds 20 ft to all MDAs [[29:229|IPH Figure 4-60]]. With no authorized setting the approach is not authorized [[33:399|AIM 5-4-5a4]].
Inoperative components or visual aids raise minimums, and ILS glideslope-out minimums are published as localizer minimums [[23:313|IFH 10-22]].
An unidentifiable stepdown fix makes its altitude the MDA, and some charts publish a second set of minimums for that pilot [[23:40|IFH 1-21]] [[33:449|AIM 5-4-20e]].
Visual segment obstacles can raise the published visibility, remove the VDP or make the procedure not authorized at night [[33:413|AIM 5-4-5i]].

body.p: **Adding visibility to an RVR value.** Convert the RVR to statute miles, add the adjustment, then convert back to the highest RVR for that visibility: 2000 RVR plus 1/8 mile is 5/8 mile, or 3500 RVR [[2:121|Chart Users' Guide p 121]].

callout.text: The IFH examples, such as ¼ mile more visibility for an ILS with the ALSF-1 out, come from an older Inoperative Components table [[23:313|IFH 10-22]] [[23:46|IFH 1-27]]. Teach learners to check the current TPP front pages, the chart notes and the NOTAMs instead of memorizing those numbers.
Highest wins: procedure, pilot, equipment [[60:471|14 CFR 91.175(b)]]. Then check category speed, altimeter source, stepdown identification, NOTAMs and notes.

check.q: Your Category B learner plans the Monroeville straight-in at 125 knots because of gusts. With the local altimeter setting, what are the minimums?
check.a: 125 knots is in Category C [[60:724|14 CFR 97.3]] [[29:148|IPH 4-8]], so the LNAV line is 840 with 1¼ miles [[23:305|IFH Figure 10-8]].

chunks.title: Altitude, airspeed and track, with the MFD's help

body.p: **Maintenance of altitude, airspeed, and track, where applicable.** You must fly the procedure to the instrument pilot skill level while instructing [[FAA-S-8081-9E:13|PTS Evaluator Responsibility]], and on final the PTS allows no more than a ¾-scale deflection of the lateral or vertical deviation indication [[FAA-S-8081-9E:11|PTS Introduction]]. The instrument standards in lesson IR.VI.A add altitude ±100 ft, heading ±10° and airspeed ±10 knots before final, and MDA +100/-0 ft to the VDP or MAP [[FAA-S-ACS-8C:21|IR ACS IR.VI.A.S9]] [[FAA-S-ACS-8C:21|IR ACS IR.VI.A.S12]].

head: Item
Technique to teach
rows: Altitude
Fix an error in two steps: stop the needle, then return at a rate about double the error; a rate more than 200 fpm off that target is overcontrolling [[23:165|IFH 7-4]] [[23:166|IFH 7-5]]
Airspeed
In a constant-rate descent the airspeed indicator is primary for power; coordinate pitch and power promptly [[23:178|IFH 7-17]]
Track, VOR
Correct toward the needle with about 20°, halve it when the needle centers, and keep bracketing the wind [[23:257|IFH 9-14]]
Track, LOC and LP

The course narrows toward the runway: a localizer is 700 ft wide at the threshold [[33:78|AIM 1-1-9b2]], and LP tightens like a localizer [[33:416|AIM 5-4-5m1(d)]]; bank no more than the degrees to turn [[23:168|IFH 7-7]]
Track, GPS
Be established before the 2 NM ramp-down; cross-track error helps when the needle seems to run away [[33:96|AIM 1-1-17b5(e)(5)]]

body.p: **Uses of the MFD and other graphical navigational displays.** An MFD can show a moving map, approach charts, terrain awareness and weather [[23:123|IFH 5-28]]. A GPS gives track, bearing, groundspeed and distance, so the pilot sees the actual track over the ground; a heading that keeps track and bearing matched takes the airplane straight to the waypoint [[23:272|IFH 9-29]]. Along-track distance finds the VDP and unnamed stepdown fixes, which may not be in the waypoint list [[33:97|AIM 1-1-17b5(e)(12)]] [[33:97|AIM 1-1-17b5(e)(13)]].

Teach the limits too. The display supplements the charts: follow the flight on the chart so a screen failure does not leave the pilot lost [[23:329|IFH 11-4]]. Pilots new to trend indicators tend to fixate on them, so use them with the primary and supporting instruments [[23:160|IFH 6-27]]. A database map of a conventional approach is position awareness, not a GPS overlay you may fly [[33:96|AIM 1-1-17b5(e)(8)]].

callout.text: Application: on a windy day, have the learner read the heading held and the GPS track on the MFD and say the wind correction aloud, then compare it with what the CDI alone showed. It ties the map to the needle and keeps the map from replacing the scan.

check.q: On final the MFD track line sits on the course, but your learner cannot say what heading they are holding. What do you teach?
check.a: The track shows where the airplane goes; the heading that keeps track and bearing matched is the wind correction to hold [[23:272|IFH 9-29]]. The display is a supplementary source, not the primary one [[23:329|IFH 11-4]].

chunks.title: The descent: rate, VDA and constant-rate technique

body.p: **Establishment and maintenance of an appropriate rate of descent during the final approach segment.** Choose a rate that reaches the MDA at a distance from the threshold that still allows landing in the touchdown zone; that point is often the VDP, and where none is charted, calculate one [[29:177|IPH 4-37]].

head: Tool
How
Example
rows: Rate from height and time
(FAF altitude - TDZE) ÷ time inbound
Rate from the VDA
Angle and groundspeed in the TPP rate of descent table [[33:414|AIM 5-4-5k3]]
Monroeville VDA 3.04° [[23:305|IFH Figure 10-8]]: 478 fpm (3.0°) to 494 fpm (3.1°) at 90 knots [[23:44|IFH Figure 1-19]]
Am I on a 3° path?
Height above TDZE = NM from the threshold × 300
Where will I reach the MDA?
MDA height above TDZE ÷ 300
IPH example 400 ft: about 1.3 NM [[29:179|IPH 4-39]]; Monroeville HAT 422: about 1.4 NM [[23:305|IFH Figure 10-8]]

body.p: **Constant rate versus dive and drive.** A constant-rate descent has many safety advantages over approaches that need several level-offs at stepdown fixes, and it keeps the approach stabilized from the FAF to landing; some countries require continuous descent final approaches (CDFAs) on nonprecision approaches [[29:165|IPH 4-25]]. FAA policy is to design approaches for stabilized, constant-rate descents, and an LNAV-only pilot flies one by choosing the attitude and groundspeed that best match the published angle [[33:418|AIM 5-4-5m7(a)]]. The VDA exists only to help the pilot fly that continuous, stabilized descent [[33:414|AIM 5-4-5k2]].

**What a constant rate does not change.** The VDA is advisory, does not guarantee obstacle protection below the MDA and changes no nonprecision rule; stepdown altitudes and the MDA still govern [[33:413|AIM 5-4-5k]] [[29:163|IPH 4-23]]. Below 1,000 ft AGL a descent rate over about 1,000 fpm is unacceptable, in the instrument or the visual part [[29:177|IPH 4-37]].

**Leveling at the MDA.** An MDA is a floor, so the descent has to stop there. Lead the level-off by about 50 ft when staying at descent airspeed, or about 10 percent of the vertical speed [[23:178|IFH 7-17]] [[23:198|IFH 7-37]]. Ballooning on the level-off and not noting the rate to set the lead are listed errors [[23:180|IFH 7-19]].

callout.text: Diving early to the MDA and then motoring along level for miles is the habit to break: it means high descent rates close to the ground [[29:177|IPH 4-37]] and more time low over obstacles. But a VDA path followed below the MDA guarantees no obstacle protection either [[33:413|AIM 5-4-5k]].

check.q: Crossing PERVE at 2,000 ft with 90 knots groundspeed, about what rate does your learner set, and about where should the MDA arrive?
check.a: About 480 to 495 fpm for the 3.04° VDA [[23:44|IFH Figure 1-19]] [[23:305|IFH Figure 10-8]], reaching 840 ft (422 ft HAT) about 1.4 NM from the threshold [[29:177|IPH 4-37]].

chunks.title: The VDP, the MDA and going below it

body.p: The VDP, a bold V on the profile, marks where a normal descent from the MDA to touchdown can begin, and the pilot should not descend below the MDA before reaching it [[2:117|Chart Users' Guide p 117]] [[33:413|AIM 5-4-5h]]. It is identified by DME or RNAV along-track distance [[33:413|AIM 5-4-5h]]; a pilot not equipped to receive it flies as if none were published [[33:413|AIM 5-4-5h2]]. VDPs apply only to LP and LNAV minima [[33:418|AIM 5-4-5m7(b)]].

Between the VDP and the MAP, a descent below the MDA may be inadvisable or impossible; speed, height above the runway, descent rate, amount of turn and runway length decide it [[33:413|AIM 5-4-5h3]]. With visibility near minimums the VGSI may not be visible at the VDP [[33:413|AIM 5-4-5h1]].

callout.text: 14 CFR 91.175(c): below the MDA only when the airplane is continuously in position to descend to the intended runway at a normal rate with normal maneuvers, the flight visibility is at least the published visibility, and at least one listed visual reference is distinctly visible and identifiable [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(c)]]. With the approach lights alone, not below 100 ft above TDZE unless the red terminating or side row bars are also visible [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(c)(3)(i)]]. Not met below the MDA, or at the MAP and after: missed approach immediately [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(e)(1)]].

body.p: There is no implicit obstacle protection from the MDA to touchdown, and the pilot must see and avoid obstacles [[33:413|AIM 5-4-5i]]. Where obstacles would push a pilot off the VDA, the chart shows "Visual Segment- Obstacles" instead, and following an RNAV descent angle below the MDA there may lead into obstacles [[33:414|AIM 5-4-5k1]]. On RNAV charts a shaded arrowhead from the VDA to the runway means the 34:1 visual surface is clear; no symbol means it is not [[2:119|Chart Users' Guide p 119]].

**Inappropriate descent below the MDA.** On the instruments it looks like the altimeter below the MDA before the VDP or MAP with no references, a push-over at the first light, or riding an advisory glidepath through the MDA. Usual causes: landing expectancy and pride, the same forces that delay go-arounds [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]; a preselector set below the MDA; a sloppy level-off. The fix: brief the MDA, VDP and MAP; set the MDA exactly, rounding up [[29:176|IPH 4-36]]; lead the level-off [[23:178|IFH 7-17]]; and go missed when 91.175(c) is not met [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(e)(1)]]. The VDP itself is a defense against visual illusions on the descent [[23:77|IFH 3-10]].

callout.text: Application: in the airplane, ask for callouts: "100 above," "MDA," "VDP," "MAP." Each one forces a decision at the right place, and a missing callout tells you where the learner's attention went.

check.q: On the Washington County RNAV (GPS) RWY 9, your learner plans to follow the GPS advisory glidepath below the MDA once the runway lights show. What does the chart tell you?
check.a: "Visual Segment- Obstacles" replaces the VDA, so a descent angle followed below the MDA may lead into obstacles, and the pilot must see and avoid them [[33:414|AIM 5-4-5k1]] [[33:413|AIM 5-4-5i]].

body.p: **Factors that should be considered in determining whether: (1) the approach should be continued straight-in to a landing; (2) a circling approach to a landing should be made; or (3) a missed approach should be performed.** Teach it as three questions the learner answers at the MDA, using the sources' own factors.

head: Decision
Factors from the sources
rows: (1) Straight-in landing

91.175(c) met [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(c)]]; flight visibility at least the published value to land [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(d)]]; enough room from the VDP or MAP for the speed, height, descent rate, turn and runway length [[33:413|AIM 5-4-5h3]]. Where only circling minimums exist, a straight-in landing is still allowed with the runway in sight early enough for a normal approach and a landing clearance [[33:449|AIM 5-4-20c]]
(2) Circle to land

Needed when it is necessary to circle the airport or maneuver for landing, or when no straight-in minimums are published [[23:311|IFH 10-20]]. Choose the pattern from airport design, ceiling and visibility, wind, final course alignment, FAF-to-runway distance and ATC instructions [[23:312|IFH 10-21]]; obey circling restrictions [[33:450|AIM 5-4-20f1]]; no circling from an RNAV (GPS) approach without an LNAV line [[33:450|AIM 5-4-20f5]]
(3) Missed approach

91.175(c) not met while below the MDA, or at the MAP or any time after it [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(e)(1)]]; an identifiable part of the airport lost while circling, except in a normal bank [[60:473|14 CFR 91.175(e)(2)]]; an approach that becomes unstabilized or an obstruction on the runway [[29:180|IPH 4-40]]; ATC directs it [[23:312|IFH 10-21]]; on a short runway with the MAP at the threshold, arriving at the MDA there may force a missed approach [[29:177|IPH 4-37]]

body.p: Circling minimums give at least 300 ft of obstacle clearance in the circling area, and the pilot stays at or above the circling altitude until in position for a normal descent to the runway [[29:149|IPH 4-9]]. If the ceiling allows, circle higher than the minimum, nearer VFR pattern altitude [[23:311|IFH 10-20]]. The circling maneuver itself is Task D, lesson FII.VIII.D.

**The missed approach.** Obstacle protection assumes the missed starts at the MAP at or above the MDA; on an early missed, fly to the MAP before turning unless ATC says otherwise [[33:450|AIM 5-4-21b]]. Climb attitude and climb power, configure for climb, turn as published, tell ATC and request further clearance [[23:312|IFH 10-21]]. Lost visual reference while circling: make the initial climbing turn toward the landing runway [[33:450|AIM 5-4-21c]]. Task C, lesson FII.VIII.C, covers the missed approach in full.

check.q: At the Monroeville MDA your Category A learner sees Runway 3 at 2 NM, but a strong wind favors Runway 21. Which line applies, and what are its minimums?
check.a: The circling line, because landing on Runway 21 needs a circle: 840-1 for Category A [[23:305|IFH Figure 10-8]]. Circling minimums apply whenever it is necessary to circle the airport to land [[23:311|IFH 10-20]].

chunks.title: Partial panel: the approach without attitude and heading indicators

body.p: The Area NOTE requires at least one nonprecision approach without the gyroscopic heading and attitude indicators, under simulated instrument conditions [[FAA-S-8081-9E:40|PTS Area VIII NOTE]]. The PTS stresses it because of fatal spatial disorientation accidents after primary instrument failures, and it asks for the failure mode most realistic for the airplane's equipment [[FAA-S-8081-9E:16|PTS Introduction]] [[FAA-S-8081-9E:11|PTS Introduction]]. The IFH tells pilots to practice flying without those instruments before a real failure [[23:333|IFH 11-8]]. Lesson IR.VII.D covers the pilot's side.

head: Item
Partial panel technique to teach
rows: Recognize
A flag, or an attitude indicator that disagrees with the turn coordinator and VSI, identifies the failure; keep control first, then cover the failed instruments and advise ATC [[23:332|IFH 11-7]]
Pitch
Altimeter primary in level flight; only small inputs; fixation on the altimeter costs heading and airspeed control [[23:197|IFH 7-36]]
Bank and heading
Timed turns on a calibrated turn coordinator, half standard rate for small changes [[23:182|IFH 7-21]]; bank no more than the degrees to turn [[23:168|IFH 7-7]]
Descent at the FAF
Without the attitude indicator, airspeed, altimeter and VSI vary until the airplane settles, so trim and control pressures must be accurate [[23:177|IFH 7-16]]
Help from ATC

Advise ATC [[23:332|IFH 11-7]]; the AIM asks for a report when an equipment failure affects safety or IFR capability [[33:377|AIM 5-3-3a1(h)]]; no-gyro vectors: standard-rate turns started at once on "turn left" or "turn right," half standard rate once on final of a radar approach [[33:431|AIM 5-4-11c3]]; a no-gyro radar approach is a major benefit when partial panel flying is required [[29:209|IPH 4-69]]

body.p: **Faulty basic instrument flying technique.** Partial panel magnifies it, because with limited instruments rapid inputs only compound a deviation [[23:197|IFH 7-36]]. Typical forms: big pitch changes that oscillate, failure to trim, chasing the VSI, no lead on the level-off [[23:178|IFH 7-17]] [[23:180|IFH 7-19]], and chasing the CDI instead of bracketing the wind [[23:259|IFH 9-16]]. Over- or under-banking the turn onto final can delay getting on course and lead to high descent rates later [[33:96|AIM 1-1-17b5(e)(4)]].

**Setting it up safely.** Brief the exchange of flight controls before flight [[25:178|AIH 9-8]], and how and when the view-limiting device goes on and off [[FAA-S-8081-9E:12|PTS Introduction]]. Application: brief how and when you will simulate the failure, too. On round dials, cover the attitude and heading indicators, as the IFH describes for partial panel work [[23:162|IFH 7-1]]. Set up as if it were real, with the primary approach NAVAID in the radio that works on battery [[29:175|IPH 4-35]]. The safety pilot needs the right certificate and adequate vision [[60:446|14 CFR 91.109(c)(1)]] [[60:447|14 CFR 91.109(c)(2)]]. The evaluator will not simulate anything that may jeopardize safe flight, and neither should you [[FAA-S-8081-9E:10|PTS Use of the PTS]].

callout.text: Application: build it simple to complex [[25:177|AIH 9-7]]: timed turns and constant-rate descents on partial panel first, then a full approach on a VOR or LOC course the learner already flies well with a full panel.

check.q: On a partial panel LOC approach your learner makes 20° heading changes by the magnetic compass and swings across the course. What do you change?
check.a: Use small timed turns on the calibrated turn coordinator, half standard rate for small changes [[23:182|IFH 7-21]], with no more bank than the degrees to turn [[23:168|IFH 7-7]]; small, precise inputs are the key with limited instruments [[23:197|IFH 7-36]].

chunks.title: Brief, demonstrate and talk it through

body.p: **Demonstrates and simultaneously explains a nonprecision instrument approach from an instructional standpoint.** The explanation must be clear, concise, technically accurate and complete with no prompting, while you fly to the instrument pilot skill level; the applicant uses a view-limiting device for this Task [[FAA-S-8081-9E:15|PTS Introduction]] [[FAA-S-8081-9E:10|PTS Use of the PTS]]. The demonstration-performance method has four phases: explanation, demonstration, learner performance with supervision, and evaluation [[25:175|AIH 9-5]].

head: Stage
What you do
rows: Ground
Objectives, completion standards and safety items before the flight [[25:175|AIH 9-5]]; teach the knowledge and procedure, practice in a simulator, then verify in the airplane [[25:174|AIH 9-4]]
Instructor tells, instructor does
Explain power settings and attitudes as you fly, in the same order as the briefing; acknowledge any deviation at once [[25:177|AIH 9-7]]
Learner tells, instructor does
The learner talks you through it, so misunderstandings are caught before the learner is busy flying [[25:178|AIH 9-8]]
Learner tells, learner does
The learner flies and thinks aloud, so you can tell a misconception from a motor-skill error [[25:178|AIH 9-8]]
Evaluate
Learner self-assessment first, then your assessment and a comparison [[25:176|AIH 9-6]]

body.p: **A talk-through you can use** (put in your POH speeds and power settings):

bullets: "Cleared for the approach and established on the NoPT leg, so the published altitude now applies [[60:474|14 CFR 91.175(i)]]. GPS armed, terminal sensitivity [[33:96|AIM 1-1-17b5(e)(3)]]."
"Two miles before the FAF the GPS goes approach active [[33:96|AIM 1-1-17b5(e)(5)]]. I am at descent speed and configured in level flight, trimmed [[23:178|IFH 7-17]]."

"FAF: power back, nose down to hold the speed, target the table's rate for the VDA and my groundspeed [[23:44|IFH Figure 1-19]] [[33:414|AIM 5-4-5k3]]. Not below a stepdown altitude until past the fix [[33:401|AIM 5-4-5b5]]."
"Fifty feet above the MDA I begin the level-off and add power [[23:178|IFH 7-17]]. Level at the MDA, missed approach altitude set [[29:176|IPH 4-36]]."

"Watching the distance for the VDP. At the VDP with a required reference and the visibility, a normal descent to land; nothing by the MAP, missed approach now [[33:413|AIM 5-4-5h]] [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(e)(1)]]."

callout.text: Positive exchange of flight controls: "You have the flight controls." "I have the flight controls." "You have the flight controls." Add a visual check, and brief it before flight [[25:178|AIH 9-8]] [[25:179|AIH 9-9]].

check.q: During your demonstration you sink 60 ft below a stepdown altitude while explaining. What should you do?
check.a: Correct it and say so right away: when a demonstration does not match the explanation, the deviation should be acknowledged and explained at once [[25:177|AIH 9-7]]. A stepdown altitude is a floor until the fix is passed [[33:401|AIM 5-4-5b5]].

body.p: **Analyzes and corrects simulated common errors.** On the checkride the evaluator flies the errors on purpose. Name the error, say what you see, give the cause and the fix, and say how you would teach it. The PTS notes that the listed errors may not appear in the references, and the evaluator will not simulate anything unsafe [[FAA-S-8081-9E:10|PTS Use of the PTS]].

head: Error
What you see
Usual cause
Fix and how you teach it
rows: Chart knowledge (K2a)
Early descent, wrong line of minima, no plan at the MAP
Briefing skipped or partial
Brief top to bottom, missed approach included, before the IAF [[29:182|IPH 4-42]] [[23:312|IFH 10-21]]
Communications and clearances (K2b)
Descent on a vector; procedure turn on a NoPT leg; no missed approach report
Not knowing when published altitudes apply; reluctance to ask
Last assigned altitude until established [[60:474|14 CFR 91.175(i)]]; no PT when NoPT [[60:474|14 CFR 91.175(j)]]; ask when unsure [[60:450|14 CFR 91.123(a)]]
Checklist items (K2c)
GPS not active at the FAWP; MDA not set; wrong altimeter setting
Workload, no flow
No descent unless approach mode is active [[33:98|AIM 1-1-17b5(g)(7)]]; brief and confirm the setup [[29:175|IPH 4-35]]
Basic instrument technique (K2d)
Altitude swings, ballooning or overshooting the level-off, CDI swings
Large pitch changes, no trim, no level-off lead [[23:178|IFH 7-17]] [[23:180|IFH 7-19]]; chasing the CDI [[23:259|IFH 9-16]]
Small corrections, trim, lead the level-off, bracket the wind [[23:257|IFH 9-14]]
Below the MDA (K2e)
Below the MDA before the VDP or without references
Landing expectancy and pride [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]; trusting an advisory angle
Apply 91.175(c) or go missed [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(c)]]; a VDA does not guarantee obstacle protection [[33:413|AIM 5-4-5k]]

body.p: Analyze before you correct: when the learner thinks aloud you can tell a misconception from a lack of motor skill [[25:178|AIH 9-8]]. Safety permitting, let a learner go partway into a mistake and find the way out, since learners who never correct an error seldom learn the maneuver well [[25:182|AIH 9-12]]. To test real understanding, vary the approach slightly or combine it with another task; a learner who only memorized will struggle [[25:182|AIH 9-12]].

callout.text: "Partway into the mistake" never includes going below an MDA or a stepdown altitude near the ground. Guard the controls and take them early; a learner must never be allowed to exceed your limits [[25:179|AIH 9-9]].

check.q: The examiner, acting as your learner, levels at the MDA and then lets the altimeter sag 80 ft while looking for the runway. Name the error, the cause and the fix.
check.a: Inappropriate descent below the MDA (K2e), often driven by landing expectancy, the same set that delays go-arounds [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]. Return to the MDA, keep the cross-check going, and go missed at the MAP without the required references [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(e)(1)]].

scenario.title: Partial panel LNAV practice into Monroeville
scenario.setup: You are a new CFII. Your instrument learner, about 25 hours into training, flies a round-dial, fixed-gear trainer with an IFR-approved non-WAAS GPS. It is a Category A airplane, planned at 90 knots on final. Today's plan is the RNAV (GPS) RWY 3 at Monroeville, a non-towered airport (Figure 10-8), with the learner under a view-limiting device and you simulating a vacuum failure before the IAF. The weather is good VMC; you are instructor and safety pilot.

questions.q: What do you brief on the ground about the simulated failure and the flight controls?
questions.a: How and when the device goes on and off [[FAA-S-8081-9E:12|PTS Introduction]], the three-step positive exchange of flight controls [[25:178|AIH 9-8]], and, as good practice, how and when you will simulate the failure. Have the learner set the approach NAVAID or GPS on the radio that works on battery, as if the failure were real [[29:175|IPH 4-35]].

questions.q: Center says "change to advisory frequency approved." What calls should the learner make on 123.0?
questions.a: The approach being flown, the position, and FAF inbound [[33:397|AIM 5-4-4d]]; the IPH adds departing the IAF and short final [[29:156|IPH 4-16]]. The learner must also arrange to cancel IFR [[29:156|IPH 4-16]].

questions.q: The CTAF gives no altimeter setting. What are the learner's minimums?
questions.a: Use the Middleton Field setting and the Middleton line: LNAV MDA 900, 1 mile, HAT 482 for Category A [[23:305|IFH Figure 10-8]]. With no authorized setting at all the approach would not be authorized [[33:399|AIM 5-4-5a4]].

questions.q: With the attitude and heading indicators covered, how should the learner start down at PERVE?
questions.a: Already at descent speed and configured, reduce power and hold the speed, aiming for about 480 to 495 fpm from the table for the 3.04° angle at 90 knots [[23:178|IFH 7-17]] [[23:44|IFH Figure 1-19]]. Without the attitude indicator the needles vary until the airplane settles, so trim carefully and make small corrections [[23:177|IFH 7-16]] [[23:197|IFH 7-36]].

questions.q: Level at 900 ft about 1.5 NM out, you lift the device. The learner sees the runway lights, pushes over and the VSI shows 1,100 fpm. What do you say and do?
questions.a: More than about 1,000 fpm below 1,000 ft AGL is unacceptable [[29:177|IPH 4-37]]. If the airplane cannot stay in position for a normal descent with normal maneuvers, it may not continue below the MDA [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(c)]]; an approach that becomes unstabilized calls for a missed approach [[29:180|IPH 4-40]]. With no VDP charted, the learner should have planned a descent point, about 482 ÷ 300 = 1.6 NM [[29:177|IPH 4-37]] [[23:305|IFH Figure 10-8]].

questions.q: How do you run the debrief?
questions.a: Collaborative assessment: the learner's self-assessment first, then your detailed assessment and a discussion comparing the two [[25:182|AIH 9-12]]. Base it on standards suited to the learner's stage, looking at each element, not just the overall result [[25:182|AIH 9-12]].

skills.do: Demonstrate a VOR, LOC or RNAV (GPS) LNAV or LP approach while explaining the briefing, setup, descent planning, the MDA, VDP and MAP decisions, and the missed approach, holding instrument pilot standards; fly at least one with the attitude and heading indicators covered [[FAA-S-8081-9E:40|PTS Area VIII NOTE]].
skills.practice: Fly the talk-through aloud in a simulator first, then in the airplane [[25:174|AIH 9-4]], in the same order every time you brief it [[25:177|AIH 9-7]]. Have another applicant act as safety pilot and play ATC [[60:446|14 CFR 91.109(c)(1)]].

skills.do: As the evaluator flies the K2 errors (chart knowledge, radio and clearance mistakes, missed checklist items, faulty technique, descent below the MDA), name each one, say what the instruments show, explain the cause and give the fix and the way you would teach it.
skills.practice: Take turns with another applicant flying the errors in the table on purpose, and correct them by thinking aloud so you separate misconceptions from motor-skill errors [[25:178|AIH 9-8]] [[25:182|AIH 9-12]].

quiz.q: Your learner asks why an LNAV approach flown with a WAAS advisory glidepath is still a nonprecision approach. What is the best answer?
options: The advisory glidepath is never shown on the chart profile
It is still flown to an MDA and has no evaluated glidepath
WAAS glidepaths are not accurate enough inside the FAF
Only ground-based NAVAIDs can give a real glidepath
quiz.why: A published VDA does not make an approach an APV, because it is still flown to an MDA and was not evaluated with a glidepath [[33:400|AIM 5-4-5a7]]. The last option is wrong: WAAS LPV gives a glidepath with no ground NAVAID and is an APV flown to a DA [[33:416|AIM 5-4-5m1(b)]] [[33:418|AIM 5-4-5m6(b)]].

quiz.q: Which RNAV (GPS) line of minima is a nonprecision line that needs approved WAAS equipment?
options: LP
LNAV
LPV
LNAV/VNAV
quiz.why: LP uses WAAS lateral guidance but is an MDA, not a DA [[33:416|AIM 5-4-5m1(d)]]. LNAV can be flown with basic GPS, and LPV and LNAV/VNAV are APV lines flown to a DA [[33:416|AIM 5-4-5m1(e)]] [[33:418|AIM 5-4-5m6(b)]].

quiz.q: On a vector your learner is cleared for the approach 10 NM outside the FAF. When may they descend to the published altitudes?
options: Right away, because the clearance includes them
Within 5 NM of the FAF, while on the assigned heading
Once established on a published route or segment
Only after crossing the FAF inbound on course
quiz.why: On a vector or unpublished route, keep the last assigned altitude until established on a published segment; then the published altitudes apply [[60:474|14 CFR 91.175(i)]] [[33:421|AIM 5-4-6h1]]. Waiting for the FAF is too conservative and not what the rule says.

quiz.q: At a non-towered airport, after "change to advisory frequency approved," what does the AIM say to broadcast on a nonprecision approach?
options: Only a short final call for traffic on the runway
A report to Center when the runway is in sight
Nothing until the IFR flight plan is canceled
Approach type, position, and FAF inbound
quiz.why: Broadcast the type of approach, your position, and when over the FAF inbound on a nonprecision approach [[33:397|AIM 5-4-4d]]. The IPH also lists departing the IAF and short final among the usual calls [[29:156|IPH 4-16]].

quiz.q: After a flap failure, your Category A learner must circle at Monroeville at 125 knots. Which circling minimums apply with the local altimeter setting?
quiz.why: 125 knots is Category C [[60:724|14 CFR 97.3]], and inoperative flaps are one of the cases where a faster speed forces the higher category's minimums [[29:148|IPH 4-8]]. Category C circling is 920-1½; 980-1½ is the Category C circling line with the Middleton setting [[23:305|IFH Figure 10-8]].

quiz.q: Monroeville's CTAF gives no altimeter setting. What does your Category A learner do?
options: Use Middleton Field's setting and 900-1
Use the GPS altitude and keep the 840-1 line
Add 100 ft to 840 and keep 1 mile
Fly the approach on 29.92 and 840-1
quiz.why: The chart note says to use the Middleton Field setting when the local one is not received, with its own line: LNAV MDA 900-1 for A and B [[23:305|IFH Figure 10-8]]. A nonlocal source may raise minimums and only the charted sources are authorized [[33:399|AIM 5-4-5a4]].

quiz.q: Your learner treats the published VDA as a glidepath to follow all the way to the runway. Which statement do you teach?
options: It is advisory; no protection below the MDA
It makes the approach an APV with a DA
It replaces any stepdown altitudes after the FAF
It must be followed exactly once below the MDA
quiz.why: The VDA is advisory, does not guarantee obstacle protection below the MDA and changes no nonprecision requirement [[33:413|AIM 5-4-5k]] [[33:413|AIM 5-4-5i]]. Stepdown altitudes still apply on an MDA line [[33:401|AIM 5-4-5b5]] [[29:163|IPH 4-23]].

quiz.q: 1 NM before the FAWP your learner's GPS still shows "armed," not approach active. What do you teach?
options: Descend anyway, since the needle is still centered
Switch to LNAV/VNAV minimums instead
Do not descend; fly to the MAWP and go missed
Set the CDI to 0.3 NM by hand and continue
quiz.why: Without approach mode the RAIM and CDI do not ramp down; do not descend to the MDA, fly to the MAWP and go missed [[33:96|AIM 1-1-17b5(e)(7)]] [[33:98|AIM 1-1-17b5(g)(7)]]. Overriding the sensitivity by hand cancels the approach mode annunciation [[33:96|AIM 1-1-17b5(e)(7)]].

quiz.q: At the VDP your learner sees flashing runway end identifier lights, has the published visibility and can make a normal descent. May they leave the MDA?
options: No, the runway itself must be in sight first
No, REIL counts only on precision approaches
Only after reaching the MAP at the MDA
Yes, REIL is one of the listed references
quiz.why: Runway end identifier lights are a listed reference, and with the visibility and a normal descent available all three conditions are met [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(c)]] [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(c)(3)(v)]]. The VDP is the point to start a normal descent from the MDA [[33:413|AIM 5-4-5h]].

quiz.q: Which telling-and-doing step lets you check a learner's understanding of the approach before they are busy flying it?
options: Instructor tells, instructor does
Learner tells, instructor does
Learner tells, learner does
Postflight collaborative assessment
quiz.why: In learner tells, instructor does, the learner explains while you fly, so misunderstandings are corrected before the learner is absorbed in controlling the airplane [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].

quiz.q: On partial panel your learner levels at the MDA and then stares at the altimeter. What does the IFH warn about?
options: Fixation can cost heading and airspeed control
The VSI lags, so the altimeter is the only guide
The altimeter is unreliable without the vacuum
Staring is fine once the airplane is trimmed
quiz.why: Rapid inputs cause oscillation, and fixation on the altimeter can lead to loss of directional and airspeed control [[23:197|IFH 7-36]]. The altimeter runs on static pressure, not vacuum: a static problem affects the airspeed indicator, altimeter and VSI [[23:333|IFH 11-8]].

quiz.q: Your learner flies the Daytona LOC BC RWY 25R on a standard VOR-type indicator. What should they expect?
options: Normal sensing, and a usable glideslope
Normal sensing once the OBS is set to 070
Reverse sensing only inside the FAF
Reverse sensing, and glideslope ignored
quiz.why: With standard VOR equipment a back course gives reverse sensing, and any glideslope signal must be ignored [[29:216|IPH 4-76]]; the chart says "Disregard glideslope indications" [[29:229|IPH Figure 4-60]].

final_quiz.q: On the Oklahoma City chart, LNAV/VNAV and LNAV both read 1580/50. What is the real difference for your learner at 1580?
options: None: both are floors that may never be broken
The LNAV line lets you sink 50 ft on a missed approach
A DA allows a brief dip on the missed; an MDA does not
The DA is a height above TDZE; the MDA is in feet MSL
final_quiz.why: Obstacle clearance allows a momentary descent below a DA while transitioning to the missed approach [[33:418|AIM 5-4-5m5(a)]]. LNAV is an MDA line, and descent below it requires 14 CFR 91.175 [[33:418|AIM 5-4-5m6(b)]]. Both are printed in feet MSL [[2:120|Chart Users' Guide p 120]].

final_quiz.q: Stepdown fix altitudes inside the final segment apply to which lines of minima?
options: Only to the LPV and LNAV/VNAV lines
Only to lines flown to an MDA
To every line of minima on the chart
Only to the circling minimums
final_quiz.why: Final segment stepdown altitudes apply when flying to an MDA line; they do not apply to LPV or LNAV/VNAV DA lines, though stepdowns outside the final segment apply to all [[33:401|AIM 5-4-5b5]].

final_quiz.q: On a VOR approach your learner cannot identify the stepdown fix on final, and the chart has no second set of minimums. What is the lowest altitude on final?
options: The published MDA, since only the FAF matters
The MSA, which protects within 25 NM
The FAF altitude until the missed approach point
The stepdown altitude, which becomes the MDA
final_quiz.why: If the stepdown fix cannot be identified, its minimum altitude becomes the MDA, unless higher circling minimums apply [[23:40|IFH 1-21]]. Some charts publish a second set of minimums for this case [[33:449|AIM 5-4-20e]].

final_quiz.q: FAF altitude 1,800 ft MSL, TDZE 300 ft, and 3 minutes from the FAF inbound. Using the IPH method, what rate does your learner plan?
options: About 400 fpm
About 600 fpm
About 500 fpm
About 700 fpm
final_quiz.why: Subtract the TDZE from the FAF altitude and divide by the time inbound: (1,800 - 300) ÷ 3 = 500 fpm [[29:177|IPH 4-37]]. 600 fpm wrongly uses 1,800 ÷ 3.

final_quiz.q: Your learner reaches the MDA 4 NM out by diving at 1,200 fpm, then flies level to the VDP. What do you teach?
options: It is the safest way, since the MDA is reached early
It is fine as long as the stepdowns were kept
Use 1,200 fpm only when below 1,000 ft AGL
Plan a constant rate; 1,000+ fpm low is unacceptable
final_quiz.why: Over about 1,000 fpm below 1,000 ft AGL is unacceptable [[29:177|IPH 4-37]], and a constant-rate descent has many safety advantages over multiple level-offs [[29:165|IPH 4-25]].

final_quiz.q: The Washington County RNAV (GPS) RWY 9 shows "Visual Segment- Obstacles" in place of a descent angle. What does that tell your learner?
options: A descent angle below the MDA may lead to obstacles
The approach is not authorized at night at all
The VDP is located at the stepdown fix ZIXEL
A WAAS glidepath is required to descend below the MDA
final_quiz.why: The note replaces the VDA when obstacles would force a pilot off it between the MDA and touchdown; following a previously published angle below the MDA may lead into obstacles [[33:414|AIM 5-4-5k1]]. Night restrictions have their own chart note [[33:413|AIM 5-4-5i]].

final_quiz.q: A VDP is published, but your learner's GPS does not show it as a waypoint. How is it found?
options: By timing from the FAF only
By the along-track distance
By the first sight of the VGSI
It cannot be used without a fix
final_quiz.why: A published VDP is not in the waypoint sequence; use normal techniques such as along-track distance [[33:97|AIM 1-1-17b5(e)(12)]]. The VDP is identified by DME or RNAV along-track distance [[33:413|AIM 5-4-5h]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner decides at the MDA, 2 NM before the MAP, to go missed. The missed approach starts with a left turn. When may they turn?
options: At once, toward the holding fix
After climbing 400 ft straight ahead
At the MAP, at or above the MDA
When ATC first gives radar vectors
final_quiz.why: On an early missed, fly the procedure to the MAP at or above the MDA before turning, unless ATC says otherwise [[33:450|AIM 5-4-21b]] [[23:40|IFH 1-21]].

final_quiz.q: On the Daytona LOC BC RWY 25R the local altimeter setting is not received. What is the Category A straight-in MDA?
final_quiz.why: The note says use Ormond Beach's setting and increase all MDAs 20 ft: 440 + 20 = 460 [[29:229|IPH Figure 4-60]]. 540 is the circling MDA [[29:229|IPH Figure 4-60]].

final_quiz.q: A procedure lists 2000 RVR and needs a 1/8 mile visibility increase. Using the Chart Users' Guide method, what is the result?
options: 2125 RVR
2400 RVR
3500 RVR
1/2 mile
final_quiz.why: Convert 2000 RVR to 1/2 mile, add 1/8 for 5/8 mile, then convert back to the highest RVR for that visibility: 3500 RVR [[2:121|Chart Users' Guide p 121]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner's airplane is certified Category B but usually flies approaches at 85 knots. Which minimums may they use?
options: Category A, because of the speed flown
Category B or higher, never A
Category A on straight-ins only
Either one; the pilot may choose
final_quiz.why: An airplane is certified in one category and cannot be flown to the minimums of a slower category, although a faster approach may require a higher one [[29:148|IPH 4-8]].

final_quiz.q: Partial panel on vectors, ATC says "turn right" for a no-gyro approach while your learner is still outside final. How should they turn?
options: Half standard rate until a heading is given
30° of bank until told "stop turn"
Standard rate at once, until "stop turn"
Wait for a heading, then use the compass
final_quiz.why: Make all turns at standard rate and start them immediately on the instruction; after being turned onto final, ATC asks for half standard rate [[33:431|AIM 5-4-11c3]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner flies the procedure turn on a NoPT leg to lose altitude without asking. Which listed error is it, and what is the fix?
options: Checklist error; add the PT to the checklist
Chart error; the PT is optional on NoPT legs
Technique error; descend faster on the leg
Clearance error; get ATC clearance for a PT
final_quiz.why: No procedure turn may be made on a NoPT route unless ATC clears it [[60:474|14 CFR 91.175(j)]]. A pilot who wants an unrequired procedure turn must first get an amended clearance [[29:183|IPH 4-43]].

final_quiz.q: Per the PTS, what must your explanation during the demonstration be?
options: Brief, so the evaluator can watch the flying
Clear, concise, accurate, complete, unprompted
Given after the approach, in the debrief
Read from a written lesson plan, word for word
final_quiz.why: Failure to give an explanation that is clear, concise, technically accurate and complete with no prompting is a typical reason for unsatisfactory performance [[FAA-S-8081-9E:15|PTS Introduction]]. The AIH says the demonstration should match the explanation and be given in the same order [[25:177|AIH 9-7]].

final_quiz.q: At the Monroeville MDA, a Category B learner must circle to Runway 21. What are the circling minimums?
final_quiz.why: The circling line reads 880-1 for Category B with the local altimeter setting [[23:305|IFH Figure 10-8]]. 840-1 is Category A and 900-1 is the Middleton line.

final_quiz.q: A learner flies perfect approaches at the home airport, but you suspect memorized patterns, not understanding. What does the AIH suggest?
options: Vary the approach or combine it with other tasks
Repeat the same approach until it is automatic
Give a written test before the next flight
Move straight on to the next lesson in the syllabus
final_quiz.why: When a learner may not understand the principles, require them to vary the maneuver slightly, combine it with other operations or apply the same elements elsewhere; those who only memorized will not succeed [[25:182|AIH 9-12]].

takeaways: Nonprecision means course guidance only: VOR, LOC, LNAV and LP go to an MDA; LPV and LNAV/VNAV are APVs flown to a DA.
Choose the approach from weather, wind, equipment and NOTAMs, then brief the chart top to bottom, missed approach included.
Authorized MDA is the highest of procedure, pilot and equipment; then raise for category speed, altimeter source and notes.
Plan a constant-rate descent from the table or timing; never over about 1,000 fpm low, and honor every stepdown on an MDA line.
An MDA is a floor: level off with a lead, leave it only with 91.175(c) met and not before a published VDP, and go missed at the MAP without it.
Teach the decision at the MDA as three questions: straight-in, circle, or missed approach.
Fly and teach one approach with the attitude and heading indicators covered, set up safely and briefed.
Demonstrate and explain in the same order, then let the learner tell and do; name each error, its cause and its fix.
cfi_notes: Classification differs by source. The AIM separates PA, APV and NPA [[33:400|AIM 5-4-5a7]]; the IPH calls APVs non-precision for alternate planning [[29:146|IPH 4-6]]; the PTS puts DA approaches with approved vertical guidance in Task B. Teach the AIM groups and the PTS split.
The IPH calls the LNAV/VNAV minimum an MDA in one sentence and a DA a few lines later on the same page [[29:166|IPH 4-26]]. The AIM publishes LNAV/VNAV as a DA [[33:416|AIM 5-4-5m1(c)]]. Teach DA.

The IPH says LP is being phased out [[29:166|IPH 4-26]], while the current AIM still describes when LP is published and how it is flown [[33:416|AIM 5-4-5m1(d)]]. Teach the AIM and mention the IPH line.

Advisory vertical guidance: the IPH says pilots, aircraft and operator must be approved to use advisory VNAV inside the FAF [[29:163|IPH 4-23]], the AIM says flying the VDA with the VSI needs no special equipment [[33:414|AIM 5-4-5k3]], and the PTS lets applicants use advisory vertical guidance without restriction. Teach it as advisory only, with the barometric altimeter, stepdowns and MDA in charge.

IFH Figure 10-8 is captioned as a VOR or GPS approach, but the chart shown is titled RNAV (GPS) RWY 3 [[23:305|IFH Figure 10-8]]. The handbook charts used here are dated 2010 to 2011; brief and fly only current charts.
IFH 1-23 bases category on 1.3 VSO only [[23:42|IFH 1-23]]; 14 CFR 97.3 uses VREF if specified, otherwise 1.3 VSO at maximum certificated landing weight [[60:724|14 CFR 97.3]]. Teach the regulation.

IFH 10-13 lists a published hold-in-lieu of procedure turn among cases where a procedure turn is not authorized [[23:304|IFH 10-13]], while the IPH says a procedure turn or hold-in-lieu is required when depicted unless ATC clears a straight-in [[29:183|IPH 4-43]] [[33:421|AIM 5-4-6h4]]. Teach the IPH and AIM.

How it is tested: the evaluator selects Tasks A and B with C, D or E, at least one nonprecision approach without the gyro heading and attitude indicators, and may ask for a landing or a missed approach after each approach; the view-limiting device is used for this Task [[FAA-S-8081-9E:40|PTS Area VIII NOTE]] [[FAA-S-8081-9E:10|PTS Use of the PTS]]. The Introduction also has the applicant fly at least two different nonprecision approaches: at least one with a course reversal, at least one from an IAF without autopilot or radar vectors, and one on backup or partial panel instruments in the failure mode most realistic for the equipment [[FAA-S-8081-9E:11|PTS Introduction]].

Examiners like to ask: MDA versus DA on the same chart, which lines need WAAS, when stepdowns apply, how to find a VDP without a waypoint, what a remote altimeter note does, and how you would set up and brief a partial panel approach safely.
gaps: AC 120-108 (continuous descent final approach) is not in the sources, so no derived decision altitude, CDFA callout or add-on to the MDA is taught here; the lesson uses only the IPH, AIM and IFH constant-rate guidance.
No source here says how to simulate an AHRS or PFD failure on a particular glass panel; use the airplane's AFM and avionics supplement for the realistic failure mode the PTS asks for.
The current TPP Inoperative Components table and rate of descent table are not in the sources; only older IFH samples are available.

The CFII PTS gives no numeric tolerances for this Task other than the ¾-scale deflection standard [[FAA-S-8081-9E:11|PTS Introduction]]; the ±100 ft, ±10°, ±10 knots and MDA +100/-0 ft figures are the Instrument ACS standards [[FAA-S-ACS-8C:21|IR ACS IR.VI.A.S9]] [[FAA-S-ACS-8C:21|IR ACS IR.VI.A.S12]], also taught in lesson IR.VI.A.
Approach speeds, power settings, configurations and checklists for a given airplane come from its POH/AFM, which is not in the sources.

activities.title: Nonprecision, APV or precision?
activities.intro: Tap each approach or line of minima, then tap the group the sources put it in.
activities.why: The AIM groups PAR, ILS and GLS as precision; LNAV/VNAV, LPV and LDA with glidepath as APV; VOR, NDB and LNAV as nonprecision [[33:400|AIM 5-4-5a7]]. The IPH adds LOC and ASR to the nonprecision list [[29:190|IPH 4-50]], and LP is an MDA line [[33:416|AIM 5-4-5m1(d)]].

activities.title: Brief the Monroeville chart
activities.intro: Drag each label to its numbered pin on the chart.

activities.why: Chart parts follow the briefing order [[29:149|IPH 4-9]]; the FAF is the Maltese cross [[2:117|Chart Users' Guide p 117]], the VDA and TCH sit in the profile [[2:118|Chart Users' Guide p 118]], and the missed approach text is in the middle briefing strip [[2:102|Chart Users' Guide p 102]]. Details are from the chart [[23:305|IFH Figure 10-8]].

Receiver says LNAV available on an LPV chart
pairs.r: Fly the LNAV line to its MDA

activities.why: Missing identifier [[33:87|AIM 1-1-11]]; localizer IDs start with I [[33:79|AIM 1-1-9b4]]; no approach mode means no descent [[33:96|AIM 1-1-17b5(e)(7)]]; RAIM after the FAWP means climb and go missed [[33:98|AIM 1-1-17b5(g)(8)]]; back course reverse sensing [[29:216|IPH 4-76]]; WAAS level of service [[33:105|AIM 1-1-18d2]].

activities.title: Minimums and descent numbers
activities.intro: Work it out, then type your answer.

items.q: Monroeville: FAF PERVE 2,000 ft, TDZE 418, 4.7 NM to RW03. At 90 knots groundspeed, about what descent rate does the IPH method give (FAF altitude minus TDZE, divided by minutes inbound)?
items.why: 4.7 NM at 90 knots = 3.13 minutes; (2,000 - 418) ÷ 3.13 ≈ 505 fpm [[29:177|IPH 4-37]] [[23:305|IFH Figure 10-8]]. The table for the 3.04° VDA gives about 478 to 494 fpm, very close [[23:44|IFH Figure 1-19]].

items.q: Monroeville LNAV MDA has a HAT of 422 ft. Using 300 ft per NM, about how far from the threshold will a 3° path reach the MDA?
items.why: 422 ÷ 300 ≈ 1.4 NM; the IPH uses the same method to find where the MDA is reached [[29:177|IPH 4-37]] [[29:179|IPH 4-39]].

items.q: Daytona LOC BC RWY 25R, Category A, Ormond Beach altimeter setting in use. What is the straight-in MDA?
items.why: 440 + 20 = 460, per the chart note to increase all MDAs 20 ft [[29:229|IPH Figure 4-60]].

items.q: Daytona LOC BC: FAF to MAP is 4.3 NM. At 120 knots groundspeed, how many seconds from the FAF to the MAP?
items.why: 4.3 ÷ 120 × 3,600 = 129 seconds, which matches the chart's 2:09 [[29:229|IPH Figure 4-60]]. Start the clock at the FAF [[29:181|IPH 4-41]].

items.q: The VDA is 3.0° and the groundspeed is 105 knots. What rate does the TPP table give?
items.why: Read the 3.0° row in the 105 knot column: 557 fpm [[23:44|IFH Figure 1-19]] [[33:414|AIM 5-4-5k3]].

activities.title: True or false: VDP, VDA and the MDA
activities.intro: Decide whether each statement is true or false.

cards.s: Your learner should not descend below the MDA before reaching a published VDP.
VDPs apply to LPV and LNAV/VNAV lines as well as LNAV.
cards.why: False. VDPs apply only to LP and LNAV minima [[33:418|AIM 5-4-5m7(b)]].

cards.s: A pilot not equipped to identify the VDP flies the approach as if no VDP were published.
Following the published VDA below the MDA guarantees obstacle clearance to the runway.
cards.why: False. The VDA does not guarantee obstacle protection below the MDA; the pilot must see and avoid obstacles [[33:413|AIM 5-4-5k]] [[33:413|AIM 5-4-5i]].

cards.s: With the visibility and a normal descent available, the approach lights alone let a pilot descend to 100 ft above TDZE without the red bars in sight.
cards.why: True. Below 100 ft above TDZE the red terminating or side row bars must also be visible [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(c)(3)(i)]].

cards.s: Between the VDP and the MAP a descent below the MDA is always possible if the runway is in sight.
cards.why: False. It may be inadvisable or impossible; speed, height, descent rate, turn and runway length decide [[33:413|AIM 5-4-5h3]].

activities.title: Straight-in, circle or missed?
activities.intro: Tap each situation at the MDA, then tap the best decision.

items.t: At the VDP: runway lights, published visibility, normal descent possible
Only circling minimums published, runway in sight early, landing clearance
Runway in sight, but the wind requires the opposite runway
At the MAP with no listed visual reference
Circling at the MDA, the airport disappears in a cloud
Below the MDA, the approach becomes unstabilized

activities.why: 91.175(c) and (d) for a straight-in [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(c)]]; straight-in landing without straight-in minimums [[33:449|AIM 5-4-20c]]; circling to another runway [[23:311|IFH 10-20]]; missed approach when the references are missing or lost while circling [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(e)(1)]] [[60:473|14 CFR 91.175(e)(2)]], or when the approach becomes unstabilized [[29:180|IPH 4-40]].

activities.title: A gyro fails on the approach
activities.intro: Put the IFH steps for a failed flight instrument in order, then tap Check.
steps: Keep control of the airplane with the instruments that agree
Speed up the cross-check and identify the failed parts
Try to restore it: power source, backup system, reset
Advise ATC, and declare an emergency if needed
activities.why: Aircraft control is maintained while identifying the failure; then restore if possible, cover the failed instruments and advise ATC before the situation deteriorates [[23:332|IFH 11-7]].

activities.title: Checkride: the examiner flies the errors
activities.intro: You are the CFII applicant. The examiner, playing your learner, flies the Monroeville RNAV (GPS) RWY 3 and makes errors on purpose. Choose what you say each time.

steps.s: On a vector 8 NM outside PERVE at 3,000 ft, right after "cleared RNAV Runway 3 approach," the examiner starts down to 2,000.
options: Let it go; 2,000 is the published FAF altitude
Name it: keep 3,000 until established on the approach
Have the examiner climb back above the MSA
Ask ATC to approve the descent on the vector
steps.why: On a vector, keep the last assigned altitude until established on a published segment [[60:474|14 CFR 91.175(i)]] [[33:421|AIM 5-4-6h1]].

steps.s: Inbound, the examiner turns 30° each time the CDI moves, swinging across the course.
options: Chasing the CDI: small corrections and bracket the wind
Fine: big corrections keep the needle centered
Switch the GPS to terminal sensitivity to calm it
Fly the heading on the MFD and ignore the CDI
steps.why: Chasing the CDI from careless heading control and no bracketing is a listed error [[23:259|IFH 9-16]]; bank no more than the degrees to turn [[23:168|IFH 7-7]].

steps.s: At PERVE the examiner pushes over to 1,200 fpm "to get down early" and levels at 840 ft 4 NM out.
options: Good technique: reach the MDA as early as possible
Fine, as long as 840 is held to the MAP
Too steep: plan about 500 fpm, a constant-rate descent
Too shallow: 1,500 fpm is the usual target
steps.why: Over about 1,000 fpm low is unacceptable, and the plan should reach the MDA where a landing in the touchdown zone is still possible [[29:177|IPH 4-37]]; a constant-rate descent is safer [[29:165|IPH 4-25]]. The table gives about 478 to 494 fpm for 3.04° at 90 knots [[23:44|IFH Figure 1-19]].

steps.s: Level at 840, 2.5 NM out, the examiner says "I see a light" and starts down.
options: Fine: any light means the runway is close
Fine, if the descent is under 500 fpm
Only with a listed reference and in position for a normal descent
Only after the examiner calls the airport in sight to ATC
steps.why: Below the MDA requires a listed visual reference, the flight visibility and a position for a normal descent with normal maneuvers [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(c)]]; a light 2.5 NM out is well before a normal descent point of about 1.4 NM [[29:177|IPH 4-37]].

steps.s: One mile before RW03, no runway in sight, the examiner gives up and starts the climbing left turn to YORUP.
options: Correct: the missed approach turn can start any time
Climb, but fly to the MAP before turning
Level off and wait for the runway at the MAP
Descend 100 ft to look under the layer
steps.why: On an early missed, fly the procedure to the MAP at or above the MDA before turning, unless ATC says otherwise [[33:450|AIM 5-4-21b]]; the GPS will not sequence past the MAWP before then [[33:97|AIM 1-1-17b5(f)(1)]].
